wellbeing.title: A short, private check-in
wellbeing.description: A brief, stepped check-in about how you have been feeling. It starts with four questions and only asks more if your answers suggest it would help. Your face is never used to infer mental health.
wellbeing.notDiagnosis: This check-in screens for symptoms and suggests a next step. It is not a diagnosis. Only a qualified clinician can diagnose a mental-health condition.
wellbeing.howBody: {{count}} questions to begin, about the last {{days}} days. More are asked only if your answers suggest a closer look would help.
wellbeing.instrumentsBody: Uses the PHQ and GAD questionnaires, which are in the public domain and widely used in clinics.
wellbeing.privacyBody: Answers stay on your device for this check-in and are not saved when you leave.

bmi.underweight: A BMI below 18.5 may mean you are underweight. A doctor can check whether this needs attention.
bmi.healthy: Keep up your current balance of activity and eating.
bmi.overweight: For Asian Indians, health risk rises from a BMI of 23. Regular activity and diet changes help most.
bmi.high: For Asian Indians, a BMI of 25 or above is the obesity range. A doctor can help you plan safe changes.

sleep.good: Keeping a consistent sleep and wake time helps maintain this.
sleep.short: Adults generally need 7 or more hours. A consistent bedtime and less screen use before bed are the usual first steps.
sleep.long: Regularly sleeping more than 9 hours and still feeling tired is worth mentioning to a doctor.
sleep.unrefreshing: Sleeping enough hours but not feeling rested is worth mentioning to a doctor.

activity.partial: Building up towards 150 minutes a week — brisk walking counts — brings most of the benefit.
activity.low: Even short daily walks count. Building towards 150 minutes a week is the target.

tobacco.none: Not using tobacco is one of the strongest things you can do for long-term health.
tobacco.occasional: There is no safe level of tobacco use. Stopping entirely gives the largest benefit.
tobacco.frequent: Stopping tobacco gives the largest single health benefit. Ask a doctor about cessation support.

alcohol.occasional: Less alcohol is better for health at every level of drinking.
alcohol.frequent: Regular drinking raises long-term health risk. A doctor can advise on cutting down.

observations.title: First look
observations.heading: The first half of your picture
observations.description: People have read the face for signs of health for a very long time. Below are the signs worth checking on your capture. Tick the ones you can actually see — you can see yourself better than the camera can.
observations.limitsTitle: Why you confirm these, not the camera
observations.limitsBody: Lighting, camera quality, skin tone and make-up all change what a photo shows. A sign you confirm yourself is far more reliable than one a phone guesses at. Nothing here is a diagnosis, and none of it should be used to decide anything urgent.
observations.checklistBody: Tick anything you can see. Tap a ticked sign to read what traditional and clinical sources associate it with.
observations.halfTitle: This is only half the picture
observations.halfBody: What a photo shows is the weaker half. Answering the questions below is what makes the report worth reading — they are what turn a visible sign into a useful direction.
observations.completeBody: You have confirmed what is visible and answered what it opened up. Your report can now use both.
observations.noSignsBody: You have not ticked any signs. That is a perfectly good result — you can go on to the full questionnaire, which does not depend on the camera at all.
observations.followUpBody: These are asked because of what you ticked above. They are the half a camera cannot see.
observations.finishToSee: Answer the questions above to continue

conjunctival_pallor.label: Pale inner eyelid
conjunctival_pallor.prompt: Gently pull down your lower eyelid. Is the inner rim pale or whitish rather than a healthy pink?
conjunctival_pallor.traditional: In Ayurveda, pallor of the eyes and skin is described as Pandu, and Pandu Roga is the classical condition that maps most closely onto what we now call anemia.
conjunctival_pallor.clinical: Pale conjunctiva is a long-standing bedside sign of low haemoglobin, and it is the sign that smartphone anemia-screening research is built on.

scleral_yellowing.label: Yellow tint in the whites of the eyes
scleral_yellowing.prompt: Look at the white part of your eyes in daylight. Is there a yellow tinge?
scleral_yellowing.traditional: Ayurveda describes Kamala as a progression of Pandu, with yellow discolouration of the eyes, skin, urine and stool.
scleral_yellowing.clinical: Yellowing of the sclera is the classic visible sign of raised bilirubin and is checked in every routine physical examination. This one is worth acting on promptly.

periorbital_darkening.label: Dark circles under the eyes
periorbital_darkening.prompt: Is the skin under your eyes noticeably darker than the rest of your face?
periorbital_darkening.traditional: Read in Darshana Pariksha as aggravated Vata with depleted reserves, usually alongside poor sleep and an irregular daily routine.
periorbital_darkening.clinical: Darkening under the eyes is described with iron-deficiency anemia, allergic rhinitis (the so-called allergic shiners), sleep deprivation, and thyroid problems. It also runs strongly in families, so on its own it often means nothing.

lip_darkening.label: Darkening of the lips
lip_darkening.prompt: Have your lips become darker or duller than they used to be?
lip_darkening.traditional: Lip colour is read in Darshana as a reflection of digestion and of the state of the colon.
lip_darkening.clinical: Darkened lips are described with tobacco use (smoker's melanosis), vitamin B12 deficiency, adrenal insufficiency, some medicines, and dehydration. Many people also have naturally darker lips.

forehead_darkening.label: Darker patches on the forehead
forehead_darkening.prompt: Is your forehead noticeably darker than your cheeks or the skin behind your ear?
forehead_darkening.traditional: The forehead is read as reflecting Agni, the digestive fire, and the regularity of daily routine.
forehead_darkening.clinical: Patchy darkening across the forehead and cheeks is described with melasma, long sun exposure, hormonal change, and some medicines.

facial_acne.label: Pimples or breakouts
facial_acne.prompt: Do you currently have pimples, and are they mostly on your forehead or along your jawline?
facial_acne.traditional: Read as aggravated Pitta and Kapha with impaired digestion. Face mapping places forehead eruptions with digestion and jawline eruptions with the hormonal cycle.
facial_acne.clinical: Acne is driven by androgens and sebum. Persistent adult acne along the jawline, together with irregular cycles, is a recognised reason to consider PCOS.

eye_redness.label: Red eyes
eye_redness.prompt: Are the whites of your eyes red or bloodshot?
eye_redness.traditional: Red eyes are read as excess Pitta, that is accumulated heat, often together with poor sleep.
eye_redness.clinical: Red eyes are described with conjunctivitis, dry eye and long screen use, allergy, and simple lack of sleep.

facial_puffiness.label: Puffy face or eyelids
facial_puffiness.prompt: Does your face or do your eyelids look swollen, especially in the morning?
facial_puffiness.traditional: Read as accumulated Kapha and Shotha, that is retained fluid.
facial_puffiness.clinical: Facial and eyelid puffiness, especially on waking, is described with kidney and thyroid disorders, allergy, and a high-salt diet.

health.sourceTitle: What this plan is based on
health.scanCaptured: Face photo analysed for visible skin and eye signs.

health.prepareBody: Note when symptoms started, what changes them, and how they affect your day. Bring your medicines, allergies and previous reports. A clinician can decide whether an examination or tests are needed.
health.safetyBody: For severe trouble breathing, chest pressure, sudden confusion, collapse, or immediate danger to yourself, seek emergency help now. Call {{phone}}. Do not wait for another scan or questionnaire.

health.incomplete: Finish your check to build a plan. Unanswered questions are not treated as reassuring answers.

reason.urgent: You reported an immediate warning sign. Stop the check and get help; this app cannot assess an emergency.
reason.prompt: You reported breathing concerns or symptoms that are getting worse. Seek advice today; use emergency help for severe symptoms.
reason.appointment: Your concern, health history or preference makes a conversation with a clinician a useful next step. Persistent symptoms deserve attention even if a photo looks normal. For a child, involve a parent or trusted adult and a paediatric clinician.
reason.routine: You did not report a current concern requiring an appointment in this check. This does not rule out illness. Seek advice if symptoms develop, persist, or worry you.

action.sleep: Try a consistent sleep and wake time. If unrefreshing sleep or tiredness persists or affects daily life, discuss it with a clinician.
action.movement: Choose gentle movement you can comfortably manage. Build gradually, within your abilities. Do not push through pain, breathlessness or worsening fatigue; ask for an adapted plan if activity is limited.
action.food: Aim for regular, varied meals using accessible local foods: vegetables, fruit, pulses and whole grains. If food access is difficult, mention it at a government health facility.
action.stress: Make time to talk with someone you trust. If stress or low mood is hard to manage, use the wellbeing check or contact a mental health professional.
action.exposure: Reduce smoke exposure where possible. For outdoor or forest work, plan rest breaks, safe drinking water and shade; discuss protective measures suited to your work with a health professional.
action.medicines: Keep a list of your conditions, medicines and supplements. Discuss new symptoms or side effects with your clinician; do not stop prescribed treatment based on this check.
action.maintain: Keep the routines that support you: regular sleep, varied meals, comfortable activity and social connection. Notice changes in how you feel over time.

gallery.title: Use a photo from your gallery

gallery.goodPhotoBody: Use the original image in soft, even front light. Face the camera directly; avoid filters, screenshots, sunglasses, heavy make-up, deep shadows, and group photos.
gallery.privacy: Opening the system picker does not give BioVision access to your entire library. Only the photo you choose enters this temporary session.

error.format: Choose a JPEG, PNG, WebP, HEIC, or HEIF image.
error.size: This image is larger than 15 MB. Choose a smaller original.
error.resolution: This image is too small to inspect. Each side must be at least 320 pixels.
error.missing: The image could not be opened. Try choosing it again.

appearance.title: What the photo shows
appearance.description: We inspect your confirmed photo automatically. You do not need to label or tick visible signs. Next, we ask about health context that a photo cannot show.
appearance.processing: Inspecting visible regions on your device…
appearance.interpretation: Compares the skin below your eyes with nearby cheek skin. Even, soft front lighting gives the clearest result.
appearance.unavailable: No appearance finding was produced. Try a clear, evenly lit photo, or continue to get a plan from your general health answers.
appearance.limits: MediaPipe locates facial landmarks. Small experimental pixel-analysis modules then compare under-eye shading, forehead tone, local reddish spots, eye-white colour, and lip-to-skin contrast. These rules are not trained medical classifiers and have no measured accuracy yet. Lighting, make-up and camera processing can change the results. No image is uploaded by this analysis.

reason.no_face: A face could not be located. Face the camera directly.
reason.multiple_faces: More than one face is visible. Take a photo of one person.
reason.lighting: Exposure or uneven light makes this comparison unreliable. Try soft light from the front.
reason.pose: Face the camera directly without tilting your head.
reason.resolution: The eye regions are too small to compare. Move closer and retake.

status.not_flagged: No clear signal in sampled areas

detail.contrast: The sampled skin below both eyes looks darker than nearby cheek skin.
detail.tone_variation: The sampled forehead patches differ in brightness. Shadows, shine or natural skin variation may explain this.
detail.local_spots: One or more small sampled areas are redder than their immediate surroundings. This does not identify pimples or acne.
detail.redness: The sampled eye-white areas show a stronger red component. Camera colour balance can affect this comparison.
detail.lip_contrast: The sampled outer-lip areas look substantially darker than nearby facial reference patches.
detail.no_clear_signal: No clear difference was found in this area.
detail.resolution: This feature occupies too few pixels. A sharper original photo taken closer to the camera may help.
detail.lighting: Shadows, very dark pixels or highlights make the comparison unreliable. Retake in even, soft front lighting.
detail.coverage: Too little usable skin or eye-white area was found. This feature is not assessed; it is not marked absent.

scope.underEyes: Shading alone cannot establish dark circles, tiredness or their cause.
scope.forehead: Only several forehead patches are compared. This is not a pigmentation diagnosis or a comparison against a preferred skin tone.
scope.spots: Only sampled forehead and cheek regions are inspected. Not an acne count; small or non-red spots may be missed.
scope.eyeRedness: Not an eye examination. Pain, light sensitivity or a change in vision needs medical advice regardless of this photo.
scope.lipTone: This cannot identify smoking or its intensity. Natural pigmentation, sun, irritation, medicines, cosmetics and image lighting can also affect lip colour.

appearance.regionLegend: Outlines show where pixels were sampled—not the borders of a condition or a diagnosis.
appearance.nativeUnavailable: Automatic photo analysis is not available on this device yet. You can still continue to general health questions and get an action plan.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body: BioVision analyses your scan on your iPhone. We do not have accounts, servers that receive your health data, advertising or tracking.

sections.heading: Camera
sections.body: The front camera is used only during a scan. Video frames are analysed in memory to measure your pulse and are never recorded or uploaded. One face photo and two eye photos are taken to analyse skin signs and estimate haemoglobin. They stay in the app's temporary storage and are removed by the system.

sections.heading: Your answers and profile
sections.body: Age, sex, pregnancy, height, weight and your answers are used only to calculate your report. They stay in memory and are cleared when you start a new scan or close the app.

sections.heading: Location
sections.body: If you choose to find nearby healthcare, your location is used on your iPhone to sort the list. It is not stored or sent anywhere.

sections.heading: Stored on your iPhone
sections.body: Only your language choice and that you accepted these terms are saved on your device.

sections.heading: Sharing
sections.body: Your report leaves the app only when you tap Share and choose where to send it. Photos are never included.

sections.heading: Third parties
sections.body: BioVision contains no analytics, advertising or tracking software, and does not sell or share personal data.

sections.heading: Children
sections.body: BioVision is designed for adults. Children under 18 should use it with a parent or guardian.

sections.heading: Changes
sections.body: If this policy changes, the app will ask you to review it again before you continue.

sections.heading: Contact
sections.body: For questions, use the support link on BioVision's App Store page.

sections.heading: About BioVision
sections.body: BioVision is a health-information prototype. It estimates health indicators from your camera and your answers and suggests which kind of doctor may help.

sections.heading: Not medical advice
sections.body: BioVision is not a medical device and does not diagnose, treat or prevent any disease. Its estimates can be wrong. Always confirm results with a qualified doctor or laboratory test, and never delay or ignore medical advice because of the app.

sections.heading: Emergencies
sections.body: If you have chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, severe bleeding, or thoughts of harming yourself, call 112 or Tele-MANAS 14416 immediately.

sections.heading: Accuracy
sections.body: Lighting, movement, make-up, skin tone and camera quality affect the results. Haemoglobin is an estimate from eyelid colour, not a blood test. Heart-rate readings are not suitable for diagnosing heart conditions.

sections.heading: Doctor directory
sections.body: Doctor and hospital details come from the hospitals' public websites and may change. Confirm timings and availability with the hospital.

sections.heading: Your responsibility
sections.body: Use BioVision only for yourself or with the consent of the person being scanned, and follow the on-screen instructions for eye photos.

sections.heading: Liability
sections.body: BioVision is provided as is, without warranties. To the extent permitted by law, the makers are not liable for decisions made using the app.

sections.heading: Heart rate and HRV
sections.body: Measured from tiny colour changes in your face using the FacePhys remote photoplethysmography model. HRV (RMSSD, SDNN), the stress index (Baevsky) and the recovery score are calculated from the beat-to-beat intervals.

sections.heading: Breathing rate
sections.body: Estimated from the slow rhythm in your pulse wave during the 30-second scan.

sections.heading: Haemoglobin
sections.body: Estimated from the colour of the inner lower eyelid (conjunctiva). The model was trained and tested on 217 adults with laboratory haemoglobin results, including 95 from India, where it identified 71% of people with anaemia. It is compared with WHO haemoglobin cut-offs for your age, sex and pregnancy status. A CBC blood test gives the exact value.

sections.heading: Face and skin signs
sections.body: Google MediaPipe locates 478 points on your face. Colour and brightness in specific areas are compared to note under-eye shading, eye redness, lip colour, forehead tone and small red spots. Face geometry is measured from the same points.

sections.heading: Lifestyle
sections.body: Sleep, activity, tobacco, alcohol and BMI are compared with WHO and Indian guidelines, using WHO BMI cut-offs for Asian populations.

sections.heading: Doctor suggestions
sections.body: Your main concern, its duration and impact, danger signs and your scan results are combined using common primary-care referral guidance (NHS, NICE, WHO) to suggest a doctor, how soon to see them and tests to ask about.

sections.heading: When results may be unreliable
sections.body: Poor or uneven light, movement, glasses, heavy make-up, a very dark or bright room, or eye photos that do not show the inner eyelid clearly.

sections.heading: 1. About you
sections.body: Age, sex, height and weight choose the right reference ranges.

sections.heading: 2. 30-second face scan
sections.body: Keep still in soft light. The app reads your pulse, heart-rate variability, stress and breathing, and takes one photo for face and skin signs.

sections.heading: 3. Two eye photos
sections.body: Gently pull down each lower eyelid so the inner pink area is visible. The colour is used to estimate haemoglobin.

sections.heading: 4. A few questions
sections.body: Tell us what is bothering you. Danger signs send you straight to emergency help.

sections.heading: 5. Your report
sections.body: See every result with its normal range, the doctor to see and tests to ask about. Find doctors nearby or share a PDF report.

sections.heading: Google MediaPipe
sections.body: Face detection and Face Landmarker models. Apache License 2.0.

sections.heading: FacePhys (Vital Camera SDK)
sections.body: Remote heart-rate models by Kegang Wang. MIT License with a privacy addendum requiring local processing, which BioVision follows.

sections.heading: Eyes-Defy-Anemia dataset
sections.body: Dimauro G. et al. Conjunctiva images with laboratory haemoglobin used to build the haemoglobin model. CC BY-SA 4.0.

sections.heading: Reference guidelines
sections.body: WHO haemoglobin thresholds (2024), WHO physical activity and BMI guidance, AHA resting heart-rate range, NHS and NICE symptom and referral guidance.

sections.heading: Healthcare directory
sections.body: Doctor and hospital listings from the public websites of Shri Mahant Indiresh Hospital, Himalayan Hospital (HIMS), Synergy Institute of Medical Sciences, Government Doon Medical College Hospital, Coronation Hospital and Max Super Speciality Hospital, Dehradun.

sections.heading: Open-source software
sections.body: Built with React Native, Expo, VisionCamera, TensorFlow Lite and other open-source libraries under their respective licenses.
